title: SRE Documentation: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Review Standards, and Runbooks
author: Maya Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose:
This document centralizes Redwood Inference SRE guidance for service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and runbooks. It is intended as the canonical reference for service owners, SREs, and on-call engineers.

Scope:
Covers all customer-facing and internal services managed by the SRE organization, including: Redwood API (hosted inference), Serving Runtime, Control Plane, Ingress/Edge stack, Metrics/Observability backends, and critical supporting systems (auth, billing, key management).

1) SLO definitions and rationale

Intro:
SLOs quantify customer expectations and guide prioritization between feature work and operational reliability. Each SLO below is paired with an error budget and an on-call response policy. SLOs are expressed at the product/service boundary visible to customers or internal stakeholders.

SLO table (core services):

| Service | SLO (Availability) | Latency SLO | Measurement Window | Owner | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| Redwood API (text-gen) | 99.95% successful requests | p95 <= 300ms for short requests (<=128 tokens) | 30 days | eng-serving-runtime | Exclude scheduled maintenance |
| Inference Runtime (GPU pool) | 99.9% capacity available for Dedicated customers | p99 tail latency <= 800ms | 30 days | eng-infra | Capacity measured at model-variant level |
| Control Plane (model routing, config) | 99.9% | API p95 <= 200ms | 30 days | eng-platform | Impacting billing/config updates requires higher durability |
| Embeddings (bulk) | 99.9% | Batch throughput >= 95% target | 30 days | eng-serving-runtime | Bulk jobs measured by job success rate |

SLO threshold rationale:
- Customer-facing text-generation has the strictest availability requirement due to interactive UX expectations.
- Dedicated capacity SLO accounts for reserved capacity commitments and must be backed by capacity planning (see section 3).

2) Error budget policy and actions

Definition:
Error budget = 1 - SLO. Track remaining error budget for each SLO on a rolling 30-day window unless otherwise specified.

Burn rate tiers and automated responses:
- Green (burn rate < 1): Normal operations.
- Watch (burn rate 1-4): Notify service owner, pause low-risk feature launches, increase monitoring frequency.
- Action (burn rate 4-8): Halt non-essential rollouts, run expedited triage meeting, allocate 1 additional SRE to mitigations.
- Emergency (burn rate >= 8): Trigger incident response playbook, notify leadership, consider temporary capacity expansion / traffic shaping.

Process when error budget exhausted:
1. Immediately open a Reliability Action item in the service board and tag with "error-budget-exhausted".
2. Convene a 30-minute triage with the service owner and on-call SRE.
3. Apply short-term mitigations (roll back release, reduce feature flags, degrade non-critical pathways).
4. Create a follow-up reliability initiative with measurable goals and owners.

3) Capacity planning

Objectives:
- Maintain headroom to meet SLOs during 99th percentile load spikes.
- Provide predictable capacity for Dedicated customers and support bursts for hosted API.

Cadence and responsibilities:
- Quarterly capacity review (owner: eng-infra, participants: eng-serving-runtime, eng-platform, finance).
- Monthly capacity health report published to SRE dashboard (metrics below).
- Pre-launch capacity verification for major features (see checklist).

Capacity metrics to monitor:
- Utilization by fleet (GPU/CPU) across AZ/region (avg, p95, p99).
- Queue lengths and request wait time.
- Prefix/KV cache hit ratio.
- Model warmup time and KV cache miss latencies.
- Reserved vs. on-demand capacity percentage for Dedicated pools.

Capacity planning checklist (pre-release):
1. Estimate QPS and token-rate for the rollout.
2. Run load test at 1.5x estimated peak.
3. Validate p95/p99 latency objectives under test load.
4. Confirm autoscaler policies and burst capacity budgets.
5. Run canary traffic with synthetic traces for 24h and review metrics.
6. Publish capacity runbook update and schedule post-launch review.

Cost-aware headroom guidance:
- Target operational headroom: 20% for hosted pools, 10% for Dedicated committed capacity.
- Use batching and caching optimizations before provisioning additional GPUs.

4) Reliability initiatives and prioritization

Overview:
Reliability initiatives are time-boxed projects created to address systemic risks identified from incidents, error budget exhaustion, capacity shortfalls, or proactive analyses.

Initiative lifecycle:
- Proposal: short doc with problem statement, impact, metrics, and owner.
- Approval: SRE manager and product manager sign-off if customer-visible.
- Execution: 2-12 week workstream with weekly checkpoints.
- Measurement: track success via defined metrics (reduce incident rate, increase cache-hit ratio, reduce p99 latency).

Example initiatives:
- "Improve KV cache hit rate for short-chat workloads" - goal: increase hit rate from 68% -> 85% in 8 weeks.
- "Autoscaler stability and safety nets" - implement cooldown and predictive scaling for bursty workloads.
- "Regional failover automation" - reduce manual RTO for region failover from 4h -> 30m.

Prioritization rubric:
1. Customer impact (error budget exposure, revenue impact).
2. Repeat incident frequency.
3. Effort vs. expected risk reduction.

5) Incident review and postmortem standards

Principles:
- Blameless culture: focus on systemic causes and corrective actions.
- Timely reviews: preliminary postmortem submitted within 48 hours; final within 7 days.
- Actionable follow-ups: each postmortem must include at least one owner-assigned mitigation and a due date.

Postmortem template (required fields):
- Title (short)
- Incident window (start/end)
- Services impacted
- Severity (P1/P2 etc.)
- Summary (what happened)
- Root cause analysis (contributing factors)
- Timeline of key events (timestamped)
- Detection and response notes
- Impact quantification (error budget used, customer impact metrics)
- Corrective actions (short-term and long-term)
- Owners and due dates
- Follow-up verification plan

Incident review cadence:
- For every P1: full postmortem + exec summary, review meeting with SRE and product leadership.
- For recurring P2/P3: runbook improvements or reliability initiative as needed.

6) Operational tooling and dashboards

Core monitoring stack:
- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex for long-term storage.
- Tracing: Jaeger for distributed traces; trace sampling rules per service.
- Logging: ELK stack (Elasticsearch + Kibana) with retained indexes for 90 days by default.
- Alerting: Alertmanager + Slack + PagerDuty integration.

Recommended dashboards (each service must provide):
- SLO health (error budget remaining, burn rate, trend).
- Capacity dashboard (utilization, queue lengths, autoscaler state).
- Latency heatmap (p50/p95/p99, tail latencies by endpoint).
- Recent incidents and unresolved RCA actions.

Alerting guidance:
- Follow the signal-to-noise rule: alerts should indicate an actionable problem.
- Two-tier alerts: page for Sev1/Sev2, notify for Sev3.
- Alerts should reference runbook steps and the on-call rotation.

Operational automation examples:
- Automated traffic shaping to reduce load on overloaded model variants.
- Automatic rollout pause if error budget burn exceeds threshold during canary.
- Autoscaling safety net that provisions additional warm instances if request queue exceeds X for Y minutes.

7) Runbooks (on-call playbooks)

Runbook structure (required for each runbook):
- Title and scope
- Owner and escalation path
- Detection symptoms (what alerts/traces/logs you'll see)
- Quick triage checklist (5 items)
- Step-by-step mitigation steps (short term)
- Recovery validation (how to confirm service restored)
- Post-incident tasks and links to postmortem template

Example: API high-latency runbook (abbreviated)
1. Confirm alert and scope: query p95 latency and request volumes.
2. Check autoscaler status and queue length: `kubectl get hpa -n inference` and `curl -s http://metrics/api/queues`
3. Inspect recent traces for increased KV cache misses or model warmups.
4. If hitting capacity, execute mitigation: a) increase replica target, b) temporarily route heavy workloads to a near-identical model variant with lower latency, c) enable degraded mode for non-critical features.
5. After mitigation, monitor SLOs for 30 minutes and then schedule postmortem if service is degraded.

Runbook hygiene:
- Runbooks must be reviewed at least every 6 months.
- After any runbook use in an incident, owner must update steps within 3 business days.

8) Ownership, review cadence, and documentation standards

Ownership:
- Every SLO and runbook must have a named owner and an escalation path. Owners are responsible for correctness and timely reviews.

Review cadence:
- Quarterly SLO review: owners validate thresholds and measurement windows; update as product requirements evolve.
- Bi-annual runbook audit: ensure coverage and fresh commands.
- Post-incident: owners close the loop on action items and mark runbooks reviewed.

Documentation standards (formatting and storage):
- Use Confluence for canonical runbooks and postmortems.
- Keep runbooks concise; use numbered steps and inline command snippets.
- Link to dashboards and alert definitions (internal links).
- Use labels: service, severity, runbook-version.

9) Quick reference: key SLAs and thresholds

- API availability: 99.95% (30d)
- Control Plane: 99.9% (30d)
- Dedicated capacity: 99.9% (30d)
- Error budget alert levels: Watch (burn >=1), Action (burn >=4), Emergency (burn >=8)
- Capacity headroom targets: Hosted 20%, Dedicated 10%

10) Appendices

A. Example CLI commands and queries
- Check current SLO burn rate (Prometheus query):
  rate(errors_total{service="redwood-api"}[30d]) / rate(requests_total{service="redwood-api"}[30d])
- List inference autoscaler status:
  kubectl get hpa -n inference -o wide
- Quick log tail (Kibana API):
  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $KIBANA_TOKEN" "https://kibana.example.internal/api/logs/search?service=redwood-api&range=15m"

B. Template: Reliability initiative proposal
- Title
- Owner
- Problem statement
- Impact metrics (before/after targets)
- Proposed solution and milestones
- Success criteria and rollback conditions

C. Glossary
- SLO: Service Level Objective
- SLA: Service Level Agreement (customer contract)
- Error budget: allowable SLO failure for a given period
- Burn rate: speed at which error budget is being consumed

Contacts and escalation
- SRE Pager: pagerduty.com/team/redwood-sre
- Eng SRE Slack: #sre-ops
- On-call roster: internal link to schedule
